analysis.one_liner: Extends every copyright term by 20 years, keeping more books, films, and music under exclusive control.
analysis.headline: The Senate Judiciary Committee approved the 20-year extension and put it on the Senate calendar, but the bill never got a floor vote before the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would add 20 years to every copyright term: works by individual authors would be protected for the author's life plus 70 years instead of plus 50, and works owned by companies would be protected for 95 years from publication instead of 75. It would also add 20 years to copyrights that already existed, and keep state-law protection for old sound recordings until 2067. It included one small exception letting libraries and archives copy works that are no longer sold commercially, for preservation and scholarship.
analysis.who_benefits: Copyright owners. Publishers, movie studios, record labels, and the heirs of authors would collect exclusive royalties for an additional 20 years on works that were otherwise about to enter the public domain — the body of creative work anyone may freely copy, republish, or build on.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Publishers, studios, record labels, and authors' heirs

how_it_helps.text: Extends copyright for works created after 1977 from life of the author plus 50 years to life plus 70 years, and for corporate-owned works from 75 years after publication to 95 years.
Adds 20 years to copyrights that already existed in 1996, so works scheduled to become public property in the late 1990s and 2000s would stay under exclusive control instead.
Extends federal protection against state-law claims for sound recordings made before 1972 to February 15, 2067, keeping those recordings under rights-holder control for two more decades.
Restores termination rights so certain authors or their heirs can take back licenses of renewal-term copyrights signed away before 1978.

analysis.who_pays: The public. Readers, libraries, teachers, filmmakers, and musicians would have paid for access to works that the law would have made free; the 20 extra years apply to works already created, so nothing new would be produced in exchange for the longer lock.
analysis.who_pays_short: Everyone who reads, watches, listens, or creates

drawbacks.text: The 20-year extension applies to works that already exist, so it gives authors no new reason to create anything; its only effect is to delay the day those works become freely available to the public.

The library and archives exception is narrow: it applies only during a work's last 20 years, only when the work is out of print and unavailable at a reasonable price, and a copyright owner can shut it off for any work simply by sending a notice to the Copyright Office.
The bill was reported out of committee with minority views filed, an indication that committee members dissented from the report.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For existing works, a longer term produces no new creativity — it is a straight transfer of value from the public to copyright holders, who would have kept collecting royalties on works already written, filmed, or recorded. The one benefit for the public, a library preservation exception, is small and easily defeated by a rights-holder's notice. An honest supporter would have to acknowledge that the gains here run overwhelmingly to rights holders and their heirs, while the public pays through delayed access and continued license fees.

outcome.mechanism: The Judiciary Committee approved it and it sat on the Senate's calendar of business, but Senate leadership never brought it up for a vote before the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Senator Orrin Hatch introduced the bill on March 2, 1995 with seven bipartisan cosponsors (4 Democrats, 3 Republicans), and it was referred to the Judiciary Committee.
The committee held hearings in September 1995, considered and marked up the bill in May 1996, and ordered it reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute.

On July 10, 1996, the committee reported the bill with a rewritten version that added a limited library and archives exception for preserving works no longer commercially exploited, and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar as Calendar No. 491.
No further action was ever taken: the bill never reached the Senate floor for debate or a vote, and the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The public came out ahead in the short run: copyright terms stayed at their existing lengths, and works scheduled to enter the public domain in the late 1990s did so on schedule. Copyright holders got nothing from this bill — though Congress passed a nearly identical 20-year extension in 1998, so the reprieve proved temporary.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public, briefly — until a similar bill passed in 1998

for.what_they_did: Pressed Congress throughout the 1990s for a 20-year extension of copyright terms, and later backed the successful 1998 version of the same extension.

against.what_they_did: Organized against repeated copyright term extensions throughout the decade, arguing they lock up culture the public has already paid to create.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's eight original sponsors split evenly across parties — Hatch, Thompson, Simpson, and Abraham (R) with Feinstein, Boxer, Heflin, and Leahy (D) — and no vote ever recorded opposition on the floor.

industries.industry: Publishers, movie studios, and music labels (copyright holders)
industries.note: The bill would add 20 years of exclusive royalties to every existing copyright, including corporate-owned works protected 95 years from publication. Those 20 years apply to works already created, so the gain comes directly out of public access: works headed for the public domain stay locked, and users keep paying for licenses.

industries.industry: Record companies holding pre-1972 sound recordings
industries.note: The bill extends state-law protection for recordings fixed before February 15, 1972 until 2067, twenty years beyond current law. Old recordings that would otherwise lose protection stay under exclusive control.

The life-plus-70 term and restored termination rights let heirs control and monetize works for two more decades. These rights flow to a small set of families and estates, not to working authors creating new material.

industries.industry: Libraries, archives, and nonprofit educational institutions
industries.note: The reported bill adds a narrow exception letting these institutions preserve and distribute works during their last 20 years of copyright, but only if the work is out of commercial exploitation and unavailable at a reasonable price — and a rights-holder's notice can end the exception for any given work. It is a small offset to a bill that otherwise extends control over the material libraries serve.
